keySentence: Being brave means doing the right thing even when you are afraid.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: The moment when the children finally confronted Grundeis at the bank was the most frightening one of all. The thief was an adult and he looked dangerous and he could have simply denied everything very easily. Emil's hands were shaking and his voice was not quite steady when he pointed and said that was the man. But he said it anyway because not saying it would have meant letting a wrong go permanently uncorrected. The policeman looked at Emil very carefully and then looked at Grundeis and then asked to see his pockets. Emil held his ground and told the truth even though he was afraid and everything he had said mattered. Being brave means doing the right thing even when you are afraid.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: The confrontation scene in Emil and the Detectives is deceptively simple but carefully constructed in its emotional truth. Emil has to accuse a grown man of theft in front of a police officer while being a child from out of town with no proof beyond his word. He has every reason to doubt that he will be believed and several practical reasons to be frightened about how the man might respond. But the alternative — staying silent and accepting the loss — would mean abandoning not just the money but his own sense of what was right. Emil had not followed Grundeis through Berlin for hours in order to lose his nerve at the decisive moment when it actually mattered most. He spoke clearly and pointed directly and told exactly what had happened in the order that it had happened without exaggerating anything. His clarity and his specificity and his obvious sincerity were themselves a kind of evidence that the policeman could not easily ignore. Being brave means doing the right thing even when you are afraid.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: The climactic confrontation in Emil and the Detectives tests Emil's bravery in its most demanding and most public form. He has been brave throughout the pursuit — choosing to act under fear, making decisions with incomplete information, trusting strangers. But following someone through the city is fundamentally anonymous bravery — the thief does not know he is being followed and watched. The confrontation at the bank is public bravery — Emil must make his accusation openly and stand behind it under scrutiny. This requires a different and harder kind of courage because it involves accepting visible responsibility for what he is claiming. If he is wrong — or if he cannot make himself believed — the failure will be public and immediate and potentially costly to him. Emil accepts this vulnerability because he knows that the right thing requires not just private commitment but public expression. Kästner suggests that this completion of private courage into public speech is what transforms moral feeling into moral action. Being brave means doing the right thing even when you are afraid.
